dataset: Religious education and worship in state schools across Europe

values.note: Strict secularism (laïcité) excludes religious instruction and worship from state schools, except in the Alsace-Moselle region.
Confessional religious instruction and worship are prohibited in public schools; optional non-confessional ethics and religions electives exist.
Public schools are secular, and religious instruction is not part of the mainstream state-school curriculum.
Compulsory non-confessional study of world religions and ethics is provided; confessional instruction and worship are prohibited in state schools.
The compulsory non-confessional KRLE subject covers Christianity, other religions, philosophies, and ethics neutrally.
Religious education is generally taught as a non-confessional subject, with provision shaped by the national curriculum.
State schools are secular; optional non-confessional religious studies may be offered if requested by parents.
Religions and ethics are taught through a general curriculum rather than confessional instruction in state schools.
State schools may provide comparative religion and worldview education within a non-confessional framework.
Religious education policy varies by canton, with comparative and non-confessional provision common in state schools.
Confessional religious education is a standard state-school subject in most Länder, paired with an optional Ethics or Philosophy alternative.
Religious education is offered by recognized religious communities, and pupils may opt out under the applicable rules.
Optional confessional religious instruction, predominantly Catholic, is offered in state schools alongside an Ethics alternative.
Catholic religious education is offered in state schools, with students able to choose not to attend and take an alternative activity.
Schools offer religious education linked to recognized faiths, with an alternative educational activity for students who do not take it.
Optional religious and moral education is available in public schools, with students free to decline the subject.
Orthodox religious education is part of the state-school curriculum, with exemption available under national rules.
Public schools provide a choice of recognized religious instruction or non-confessional ethics, depending on the education network.
Pupils generally receive religious education based on their own faith community, with secular ethics available to some pupils.
Religious education may be offered in state schools as an optional subject, while ethics or civic education provides alternatives.
Pupils choose between religious education and ethics as alternative subjects in state schools.
State schools provide religious or ethics education, with families choosing the applicable option.
Catholic religious education is commonly offered as an optional subject, with Ethics available as an alternative.
Religious education is provided in public schools with participation and withdrawal governed by national rules.
Optional Orthodox and other religious education is available in state schools under the national curriculum.
Pupils may choose religious instruction from recognized faiths or ethics in state schools.
Religious instruction is available in state schools under defined conditions, with ethics or other study available as an alternative.
Catholic religious education is taught in state schools, and students may opt out under the applicable rules.
Orthodox religious education is included in state-school provision, with exemption arrangements available.
Ethics and citizenship education is provided as a common subject in public schools, replacing earlier denominational instruction.
Statutory Religious Education plus daily collective worship in England, Wales, and Northern Ireland (Religious Observance in Scotland) includes a parental opt-out.
State-funded primary schools are predominantly denominational, mostly under Catholic patronage, with a constitutional right to opt out of religious instruction.
